questions.question: What does $A\cup B$ mean for two events $A$ and $B$?
options: At least one of $A$ or $B$ occurs
questions.explanation: $A\cup B$ occurs when at least one of $A$ or $B$ occurs (including both).
questions.source_support: The definition says $A\cup B$ is the event that at least one of $A$ or $B$ occurs.

'Neither occurs' is $(A\cup B)^c$.
'Only $A$, not $B$' is $A\cap B^c$, just part of the union.

questions.question: $A\cap(B\cup C)$ equals:
questions.explanation: Intersection distributes over union: $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$.
questions.source_support: Distributive law for events.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: $(A\cap B)\cap(A\cap C)$ uses intersection where union is needed; it equals $A\cap B\cap C$.
$A\cup(B\cap C)$ swaps the roles of $\cap$ and $\cup$.
$(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)$ is the other distributive law, for $A\cup(B\cap C)$.

questions.question: For any events, $A\cap B$ is always:
questions.explanation: Every outcome of $A\cap B$ lies in $A$ (and in $B$), so $A\cap B\subseteq A$.
questions.source_support: $A\cap B\subseteq A\subseteq A\cup B$.

The intersection is a SUBSET of $A$, not a superset.
$A\cap B$ overlaps $A$ (it is part of $A$), so it is not disjoint from $A$ unless empty.

questions.question: Why does $P(A)+P(B)$ usually overcount $P(A\cup B)$?

The union excludes all outcomes in the intersection
Outcomes in $A\cap B$ are counted once in $P(A)$ and once in $P(B)$
